bottle.name: Maker's Mark Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whisky

bottle.mash: By the distillery's own account 70 per cent corn, 16 per cent soft red winter wheat and 14 per cent malted barley: wheat stands where most bourbons use rye.

bottle.pour: Neat, with a few drops of water or over one large cube. It makes a gentle Old Fashioned and stands in a Whiskey Sour, a Gold Rush and a Mint Julep.

records.table: Maker's Mark is the wheated bourbon from Loretto, Kentucky, made with soft red winter wheat where most bourbons use rye. The bottle with the red wax is its Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whisky at 90 proof: caramel, vanilla and cherry, soft enough for a gentle Old Fashioned.
records.story: Bill Samuels Sr. (died 1992) bought the old Burks' Distillery at Loretto in the autumn of 1953, and distilling began there the following year. He built his recipe around soft red winter wheat in place of rye, and the first bottles went on sale in 1958. His wife, Margie Samuels (died 1985), is credited with the name, the label, the shape of the bottle and the red wax that seals each neck, an idea said to be drawn from her collection of old Cognac bottles. In 1980 the distillery, listed as Burks' Distillery, was made a National Historic Landmark. The family sold the business to Hiram Walker & Sons in 1981 and went on managing it. The brand passed to Fortune Brands in 2005, and in 2014 Beam, the company that then held it, was sold to Suntory of Japan. Through every change the recipe and the single strength stayed as they were. For a bartender the bottle is the plain lesson in wheat: one mash, one strength, and the wheated bourbon that nearly every bar carries.

records.table: Made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort, W. L. Weller is a line of wheated bourbons, and Weller Special Reserve is its green label at 90 proof. With wheat in the place of rye it pours honey, caramel and butterscotch, a soft bourbon for the guest who finds rye too peppery.
records.story: The label carries the name of William Larue Weller (1825 to 1899), who went into the whiskey trade in Louisville in 1849 with his brother, as W. L. Weller & Brothers. The brand credits him with putting wheat in the mash where others used rye, though historians have long debated whether he distilled at all. In 1893 the firm hired a young salesman, Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle (1874 to 1965), who bought it with a fellow salesman in 1908 and later joined it to the A. Ph. Stitzel distillery. The Stitzel-Weller Distillery opened near Louisville on Derby Day in 1935 and made the wheated recipe its own. The Van Winkle family sold the distillery to Norton Simon in 1972, the stills there went quiet in the early 1990s, and in 1999 the Weller label was bought by the Sazerac Company, which moved it to Buffalo Trace in Frankfort. Special Reserve is the first step of the range that followed, and the bottle a guest who asks for a wheater is most often poured.

records.table: Pappy Van Winkle is a wheated bourbon made at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort to the Van Winkle family's recipe from the old Stitzel-Weller distillery. The Family Reserve 15 Year Old is the one a guest means: fifteen years in oak at 107 proof, caramel, leather and spice, poured neat.
records.story: Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle (1874 to 1965) began in 1893 as a salesman for W. L. Weller & Sons of Louisville. In 1908 he and a fellow salesman bought the firm; they later merged it with the A. Ph. Stitzel distillery, and on Derby Day in 1935 Stitzel-Weller opened, its bourbons built on wheat where others used rye. His son, Julian Van Winkle Jr. (died 1981), was pressed by stockholders to sell the distillery in 1972, and afterwards revived a label from before Prohibition, Old Rip Van Winkle, bottling whiskey from the old distillery's stocks. The founder's grandson carried the business on from 1981, bottling aged wheated bourbon, and in 1994 released a 20 year old named for his grandfather: Pappy Van Winkle's Family Reserve. In 2002 the family entered a joint venture with Buffalo Trace, which has distilled the whiskey since; the last Stitzel-Weller stocks went into bottles during the years that followed. The 15 Year Old, at 107 proof, is the bottling most guests mean when they ask for Pappy.

records.table: Named for the Treasury agent of the Old Fitzgerald legend, Larceny is a wheated bourbon that Heaven Hill makes in Louisville. The Small Batch at 92 proof tastes of fresh bread, toffee and buttery caramel, the wheater to pour when Maker's Mark or Weller is not the answer.
records.story: The name comes from a legend told about Old Fitzgerald, the wheated bourbon that was the flagship of Stitzel-Weller. John E. Fitzgerald, the story goes, was no distiller but a Treasury agent, one of the few men allowed the keys to a bonded warehouse, and he used them to draw whiskey from the barrels he liked; the lightened casks were known as Fitzgerald barrels. The Old Fitzgerald name dates from the nineteenth century, and Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle (1874 to 1965) made it a wheated bourbon at Stitzel-Weller after Prohibition. When that distillery fell silent in the early 1990s the bourbon moved to the new Bernheim Distillery in Louisville, and in 1999 Bernheim and the brand were sold to Heaven Hill, three years after the fire of 1996 at its own distillery in Bardstown. Heaven Hill launched Larceny in 2012 on the Fitzgerald story, with a keyhole cut into the label, and a barrel proof version followed in 2020. Its keyhole label makes the legend easy to tell to a guest who wants a wheater beyond the better known names.

records.story: By the brand's account the name first appeared in 1870, on a whiskey a Milwaukee liquor merchant sold to steamships, railways and private clubs, and only later on general sale. As Prohibition ended the name passed to Julian "Pappy" Van Winkle and his partners, and when their Stitzel-Weller Distillery opened near Louisville in 1935, Old Fitzgerald became its main bourbon, made with wheat in place of rye; the plant was often called the Old Fitzgerald Distillery. The Van Winkle family sold the distillery in 1972, and the label went with it through a line of drinks companies. Distilling at Stitzel-Weller ended in the early 1990s and the recipe moved to the new Bernheim Distillery in Louisville; in 1999 Heaven Hill bought Bernheim from Diageo, and with it the Old Fitzgerald name and its barrels. In 2018 Heaven Hill began a twice yearly series of aged, bonded decanters, each edition of its own age, and in June 2025 it launched the 7 Year Old as the label's standing bottling. Behind a bar it is the wheater that carries the Stitzel-Weller name, at the strength the bond demands.

The 7 Year Old and the decanter series are different bottlings: the decanters change their age with each spring and fall edition.
Bottled-in-Bond promises at least four years, one season and 100 proof; the seven years is the label's own age statement on top of it.

report: Written on 2026-11-22 in Rebel's place, after the owner took Rebel out as a label a fine dining guest does not ask for; Rebel's record and its checked block are gone with it, and its lines in reviews/wheated-bourbon.json were not touched by this run.

Flagship: the 7 Year Old Bottled-in-Bond, launched in June 2025 as the label's standing bottling (Heaven Hill's release, Whisky Advocate, VinePair, The Whiskey Wash), chosen over the decanter series because the decanters change age with each spring and fall edition and the 7 Year Old can be poured all year.

Bottle name: retail listings print Old Fitzgerald Aged 7 Years Bottled-In-Bond Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey while Heaven Hill writes 7 Year Old; a refuter should read the bottle and set the name to its words.

The merchant who first sold the whiskey is Solomon Charles Herbst in Wikipedia and Heaven Hill's timeline, but no two sources give his death, so he is described and not named; the year he registered the name is 1884 or 1901 by Heaven Hill's own pages and is left out, as is the year 1933 for the sale to the Stitzel-Weller partners, which the two sources read attach to different events.

Left out for want of a source: the sum paid for the name after Prohibition (excluded by the voice in any case), the drinks companies between 1972 and 1999 by name (Wikipedia's chain is garbled), the still type at Bernheim, and the warehouse the barrels age in.

Bernheim as the still: Heaven Hill says its wheated bourbon has been made there continually since 1999, and a seven year old of 2025 was distilled about 2018, before the return to Bardstown announced in 2022 that the Larceny refuter met.

Larceny's record in this group lists Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond under others, as Heaven Hill's older wheated label; with Old Fitzgerald now its neighbour here, the integrator may wish to drop or reword that entry. Larceny's story also tells the Old Fitzgerald history from Pappy to the 1999 sale, so this story opens on 1870 and tells the later years briefly.

No living person is named. The tasting words are Heaven Hill's own; three reviews read through search agree on honey, cinnamon and oak. The label term Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey rests on retail listings of the bottle and on the class of a bonded bourbon of seven years; Heaven Hill's release names Bottled-in-Bond and Your Key to Hospitality on the label.
